title: Letters & Interviews: Real-World Voices
description: Master formal and informal letter conventions, adapt your register to audience and purpose, plan and conduct interviews, and turn what people tell you into accurate, engaging articles.

notes.heading: Formal vs Informal Letters
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A letter's formality is set by its purpose and audience. Formal letters go to people you do not know personally or to organisations; informal letters go to friends and family.

🔑 Key Concept
Formal letters:
• Written for a practical purpose — to complain, apply, request or inform.
• Use Standard English, full sentences and no slang or contractions.
• Get to the point politely and quickly.
Informal letters:
• Written to share news, invite, thank or keep in touch.
• May use contractions, dashes, exclamations and a chatty voice.
• Still need a clear structure so the reader can follow.

💡 Worked Example
Formal opening: 'I am writing to request a refund for a coat purchased from your Harbour Street branch on 4 May.'
Informal opening: 'Guess what — the coat saga continues! You'll never believe what the shop said.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Decide audience and purpose before you write a word.
• The same events can be reported formally or informally — the facts stay, the voice changes.
• Exam tasks usually state the audience; underline it.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drifting between registers — starting formally ('I am writing to complain') and ending chattily ('Anyway, sort it out, yeah?'). Pick a register and hold it.

notes.heading: Letter Layout and Conventions
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Letter conventions are the standard features of layout — addresses, date, salutation and sign-off — that signal formality and help the letter do its job.

🔑 Key Concept
A formal letter includes:
• Your address (top right) and the recipient's name and address (left, below).
• The date.
• A salutation: 'Dear Sir or Madam' if you do not know the name; 'Dear Ms Chen' if you do.
• A subject line or clear first sentence stating your purpose.
• The sign-off: 'Yours faithfully' after 'Dear Sir or Madam'; 'Yours sincerely' after a named person.
An informal letter needs only your address (or just the place), the date, 'Dear...' and a friendly sign-off like 'Best wishes' or 'Love from'.

💡 Worked Example
'Dear Sir or Madam, ... Yours faithfully, A. Okafor' — but 'Dear Mr Reyes, ... Yours sincerely, A. Okafor'.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Faithfully = unnamed recipient; sincerely = named recipient. Never mix them.
• Clear paragraphs: one idea each, with the purpose in the first.
• Sign your name, and print it underneath in formal letters.

✅ Check
Cover your salutation. Could a stranger still tell from your sign-off whether you knew the recipient's name?

notes.heading: Register and Audience
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Register is the level of formality in your language. It is controlled by vocabulary, sentence structure and tone, and it must match your audience and purpose.

🔑 Key Concept
Formal register markers:
• Full forms ('I am', 'do not') instead of contractions.
• Precise, neutral vocabulary ('request', 'dissatisfied') rather than slang ('gutted', 'well dodgy').
• Politeness structures: 'I would be grateful if...', 'I look forward to your reply.'
Informal register markers:
• Contractions, idioms and direct address.
• Shorter, looser sentences.
• Personal asides and humour.

💡 Worked Example
Same message, two registers:
Formal: 'I trust the matter can be resolved promptly.'
Informal: 'Fingers crossed they sort it out soon!'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Register is a dial, not a switch — you can be politely warm without slang.
• Vocabulary choice is the fastest way to shift register.
• Being formal never means being rude; firm and polite go together.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking formal means long-winded. 'I am writing to inform you that I wish to make an enquiry regarding...' says nothing — formal can still be direct.

notes.heading: Letters of Complaint, Application and Thanks
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Three common formal letter types each have a clear job: a complaint seeks to put something right, an application asks to be considered, and a thank-you letter acknowledges help or a gift.

🔑 Key Concept
Complaint:
• State what happened, when and where, with key facts.
• Explain the impact calmly.
• Say what you want done (refund, replacement, apology).
Application:
• Name the role or opportunity and where you saw it.
• Match your skills and experience to what they asked for, with evidence.
• Close with enthusiasm and availability.
Thanks:
• Be specific about what you are thanking them for and the difference it made.

💡 Worked Example
Complaint core: 'When the tent leaked during its first use, I returned it to your branch, where I was told no refund was possible. I would now like a full refund of £60.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Facts first, feelings second, request last — in that order.
• Anger weakens a complaint; calm precision strengthens it.
• In applications, every claim needs a specific example behind it.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a complaint that rants for three paragraphs but never states what you actually want the reader to do.

notes.heading: Planning and Conducting an Interview
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An interview is a structured conversation designed to gather information, experiences or opinions from one person. Good interviews are planned but flexible.

🔑 Key Concept
Before:
• Research your subject so you do not ask what you could have looked up.
• Prepare open questions (who, what, why, how, 'tell me about...') rather than closed ones answerable with 'yes' or 'no'.
• Order questions from easy warm-ups to deeper ones.
During:
• Listen actively — the best question is often a follow-up to something they just said ('You mentioned the first match was tough — what happened?').
• Take brief notes or ask permission to record.
• Do not interrupt a good answer to get to your next scripted question.

💡 Worked Example
Closed: 'Do you enjoy coaching?' Open: 'What keeps you coaching after fifteen years?' — the second invites stories, not a one-word answer.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Open questions get material; follow-up questions get the gold.
• Silence is a tool — people often fill a pause with their best answer.
• Note exact words for anything you might quote.

✅ Check
Read each planned question aloud. Can it be answered in one word? If so, rewrite it.

notes.heading: Turning an Interview into an Article
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A profile or interview article shapes raw interview material into a story for readers. The interviewee provides the voice; the writer provides the structure.

🔑 Key Concept
• Find the angle — the single most interesting thread of the interview — and lead with it.
• Structure: hook (a striking quote or moment), background, the main story with quotes woven in, and a closing that looks forward or circles back.
• Weave quotation and paraphrase: quote the words that are vivid or revealing; paraphrase routine information to keep pace.
• Add observation — what the person and setting looked and sounded like — so readers feel present.

💡 Worked Example
Raw answer: 'Well, I suppose the night we won the cup with ten players, that was the best, because nobody thought we could.'
Article line: 'Ask her for one highlight and she does not hesitate: winning the cup "with ten players... nobody thought we could."'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The article is about the person, not about you asking questions — cut 'then I asked'.
• Keep quotes short and punchy; two lines is usually plenty.
• Every quote must be accurate — see the ethics note.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a transcript with an introduction stapled on. An article selects and shapes; a transcript just repeats.

notes.heading: Ethics and Accuracy
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Anyone who quotes or writes about real people has responsibilities: to get words right, to be fair, and to respect the person behind the story.

🔑 Key Concept
• Permission — tell people you are interviewing them and how you will use what they say; ask before recording.
• Accuracy — quote exactly what was said. Never 'improve' someone's grammar inside quotation marks; paraphrase instead if the wording is messy.
• Context — a quote cut out of context can twist someone's meaning; keep enough of the surrounding sense.
• Checking — offer to read quotations back, correct spellings of names, and verify facts you are unsure about.
• Respect — if someone asks that something stay private, honour it; a good article is not worth betraying trust.

💡 Worked Example
If your interviewee said 'It was, like, the scariest thing ever, honestly', you may paraphrase ('she called it the most frightening experience of her life') or quote selectively ('the scariest thing ever') — but you may not rewrite it as a polished sentence inside quotation marks.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Quotation marks are a promise: these were the exact words.
• Paraphrase lets you tidy up; quotation does not.
• Getting names, dates and places right is part of respect.

✅ Check
Before publishing anything, ask: would the interviewee recognise their own words and meaning here?

flashcards.definition: A letter to an organisation or someone you do not know personally, using Standard English and conventional layout.
flashcards.example: A letter to a bus company requesting a refund for a cancelled service.

flashcards.definition: A letter to a friend or family member that may use contractions, idioms and a chatty voice.
flashcards.example: A letter to your cousin describing your first week at a new school.

flashcards.definition: The opening greeting of a letter, such as 'Dear Sir or Madam' or 'Dear Ms Chen'.
flashcards.example: Use 'Dear Sir or Madam' when you do not know the recipient's name.

flashcards.definition: Formal sign-offs: 'faithfully' after an unnamed salutation ('Dear Sir or Madam'), 'sincerely' after a named one ('Dear Mr Reyes').
flashcards.example: 'Dear Dr Novak, ... Yours sincerely' — never 'Yours faithfully' to a named person.

flashcards.definition: The level of formality in language, shown through vocabulary, sentence structure and tone.
flashcards.example: 'I would be grateful if...' is formal register; 'Any chance you could...?' is informal.

flashcards.definition: A formal letter that states what went wrong, explains its impact, and asks for a specific remedy.
flashcards.example: Facts first, feelings second, request last: 'The tent leaked on first use... I would like a full refund of £60.'

flashcards.definition: A formal letter asking to be considered for a role or opportunity, matching your skills to what is asked for.
flashcards.example: Applying for a weekend job by describing your reliability and giving an example of responsibility.

flashcards.definition: A question that invites a full answer and cannot be answered with one word.
flashcards.example: 'What keeps you coaching after fifteen years?' rather than 'Do you like coaching?'

flashcards.definition: A question answerable with 'yes', 'no' or a single fact — useful for checking details but poor for gathering stories.
An unscripted question that responds to something the interviewee has just said, digging deeper.
flashcards.example: 'You said the first match was tough — what exactly happened that night?'

flashcards.definition: The single most interesting thread of an interview, chosen to lead and shape the article.
flashcards.example: From an hour with a coach, the angle might be the cup win with ten players, not her whole career history.

flashcards.definition: Paraphrase restates someone's meaning in your own words; quotation repeats their exact words inside quotation marks and must be word-perfect.
flashcards.example: Messy spoken words can be paraphrased ('she called it terrifying') but never tidied up inside quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which salutation should you use in a formal letter when you do not know the recipient's name?
choices: Dear friend
Dear Sir or Madam
Hi there
To whom it may concern, lol
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam' is the standard formal salutation for an unnamed recipient; it pairs with the sign-off 'Yours faithfully'.

questions.stem: A letter beginning 'Dear Ms Chen' should end with:
choices: Yours faithfully
See ya
Yours sincerely
To be continued
questions.explanation: When the recipient is named, the correct formal sign-off is 'Yours sincerely'. 'Yours faithfully' is only for 'Dear Sir or Madam'.

choices: A question with no answer
A question that invites a full, detailed answer rather than 'yes' or 'no'
A question asked in public
A question the interviewer has not prepared
questions.explanation: Open questions ('what', 'how', 'why', 'tell me about...') draw out stories and opinions, which is the raw material of a good interview.

questions.stem: Which of these is a marker of formal register?
choices: Contractions like 'can't' and 'won't'
Slang and text-speak
Phrases such as 'I would be grateful if you could...'
Lots of exclamation marks
questions.explanation: Politeness structures, full forms and precise vocabulary mark formal register; contractions, slang and heavy exclamation belong to informal writing.

questions.stem: In an interview article, what is the 'angle'?
choices: The camera position used for the photo
The single most interesting thread, chosen to lead and shape the article
The list of questions in the order they were asked
The writer's opinion of the interviewee
questions.explanation: The angle is the editorial choice of what the story is really about — it decides the hook, the structure and what gets left out.

questions.stem: Which sentence is most appropriate for a formal letter of complaint?
choices: Your service was absolutely rubbish and I'm fuming.
I am writing to express my dissatisfaction with the repair carried out on 12 June and to request a full refund.
You lot need to sort this out ASAP!!!
Hey, so basically the thing you fixed broke again, whatever.
questions.explanation: A complaint is strongest when it is calm, factual and states the remedy sought. Slang, insults and ranting weaken the case and break the formal register.

questions.stem: Which is the best follow-up question after an interviewee says: 'The night shift changed how I see this town'?
choices: Next question: what is your favourite food?
So you agree night shifts are bad?
Changed it how — what did you see that surprised you most?
OK. Moving on now.
questions.explanation: A good follow-up picks up the interviewee's own words and digs deeper. Option B puts words in their mouth; A and D abandon a promising thread.

questions.stem: Why should you research your subject before an interview?
choices: So you can show off how much you know
To avoid wasting time on questions you could have answered yourself, freeing the interview for deeper material
Because interviewees refuse unprepared interviewers
Research is not necessary if your questions are good
questions.explanation: Basic facts are available elsewhere; interview time is precious and should be spent on experience, opinion and story that only the person can provide.

questions.stem: An interviewee said: 'It was, like, the scariest thing ever, honestly.' What may a writer ethically do?
choices: Quote it as: 'It was the scariest thing ever.'
Paraphrase it — 'she called it the most frightening experience of her life' — or quote the words exactly as spoken
Invent a more dramatic quote and attribute it to her
Quote it but change 'scariest' to 'most terrifying' inside the quotation marks
questions.explanation: Quotation marks promise the exact words, so tidying up inside them is a breach of trust. Paraphrase lets you report the meaning accurately in your own words.

questions.stem: In a formal letter of application, what should support each claim about your skills?
choices: A compliment about the company
A specific example or piece of evidence
A list of your hobbies
An apology for any weaknesses
questions.explanation: Claims without evidence are just adjectives. 'I am reliable' persuades no one; 'I have opened my aunt's café every Saturday for a year' does.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits an informal letter to a friend about a concert?
choices: I am writing to inform you of my attendance at a musical performance.
To whom it may concern, the concert was satisfactory.
You will NOT believe who I saw on Saturday — I still can't hear properly!
Dear Sir or Madam, I recently attended a concert.
questions.explanation: The informal register allows contractions, direct address and excitement. Options A, B and D are all formal conventions aimed at the wrong audience.

questions.stem: Which paragraph order gives a letter of complaint the strongest structure?
choices: Demand → vague anger → background of the company → your life story
What happened and when → the impact on you → what you want done
What you want → what happened → a joke to lighten the mood
The impact → your opinion of the staff → a threat to go to the newspapers
questions.explanation: Facts first, feelings second, request last lets the reader verify the problem, understand why it matters, and see exactly how to resolve it — calm precision beats anger.

questions.stem: During an interview, the interviewee gives a long, fascinating answer about an unexpected topic. Your next scripted question is on something else entirely. What should a skilled interviewer do?
choices: Interrupt politely and return to the script
Let them finish, then ask a follow-up about the unexpected topic before gently returning to the plan
End the interview early — the plan is ruined
Pretend to take notes and ignore the answer
questions.explanation: Interviews should be planned but flexible. The best material is often unscripted; active listening means following gold when it appears, then steering back.

questions.stem: A profile article includes the line: 'Ask him about the flood, and he goes quiet. "We lost everything in one night," he says, turning his mug in slow circles.' Why is this more effective than quoting the interview at length?
choices: It is not — longer quotes are always better
It combines a short, vivid quotation with observed detail and the writer's framing, so readers see the scene rather than read a transcript
It avoids using the interviewee's actual words, which is safer
It makes the article shorter, which is the only goal
questions.explanation: Strong profiles weave brief quotes with observation and framing. The turned mug and the pause carry emotion that a long transcript would dilute.

questions.stem: An interviewee tells you a moving personal story, then asks you not to publish it. What is the ethical response?
choices: Publish it anyway — once said aloud, it is public
Publish it but change their name slightly so nobody can tell
Respect the request and leave the story out, finding other material for the article
Quote it as coming from 'a source' instead
questions.explanation: Ethical writing respects the person behind the story. Disguising a withdrawn story still betrays trust; honouring the request protects both them and your credibility.
